new.q: [Meteorology | Upper air, soundings, CAPE | Tier 7] A dry parcel at 35 °C rises 3 km without condensation. What is its temperature (°C)?
new.w: Using the environmental lapse rate (about 6.5 °C/km) instead of the parcel’s own rate.
sol: Rising air expands and cools.
Dry adiabatic lapse rate is 9.8 °C per km.
T = 35 − 9.8×3 = 5.6 °C. Trap: Using the environmental lapse rate (about 6.5 °C/km) instead of the parcel’s own rate.

new.q: [Meteorology | Severe-weather clouds | Tier 7] The surface temperature is 30 °C and the dew point is 18 °C. About how high (m) is the lifting condensation level (cloud base)?
new.w: Using the lapse rate (9.8 °C/km) without noting that the dew point also falls slightly.
sol: Cloud base sits where the temperature falls to the dew point.
Rule of thumb: about 125 m per °C of the temperature–dew-point spread.
LCL ≈ 125×(30−18) = 1.5e+03 m. Trap: Using the lapse rate (9.8 °C/km) without noting that the dew point also falls slightly.

new.q: [Meteorology | Tornadoes and radar | Tier 9] A radar pulse returns 2 ms after it was sent. How far away (km) is the echo?
new.w: Forgetting the factor of 2 doubles the range (partial-step trap).
sol: The pulse goes out and back.
Range = c·t/2, with c = 3×10⁸ m/s.
R = (3×10⁸ × 2×10⁻³)/2 = 3e+05 m = 300 km. Trap: Forgetting the factor of 2 doubles the range (partial-step trap).

new.q: [Meteorology | Tornadoes and radar | Tier 11] A velocity couplet shows 20 kt inbound next to 40 kt outbound. What is the rotational velocity (kt)?
new.w: Dividing the SUM by two gives the mean motion of the storm, not its rotation.
sol: Rotation has equal and opposite parts.
Vrot = (V_out − V_in)/2, with inbound written as negative.
Vrot = (40 − (-20))/2 = 30 kt. Trap: Dividing the SUM by two gives the mean motion of the storm, not its rotation.

new.q: [Meteorology | Upper air, soundings, CAPE | Tier 12] A sounding shows CAPE = 2000 J/kg. What is the theoretical maximum updraft speed (m/s) from w = √(2·CAPE)?
new.w: Real updrafts are well below this because of entrainment and drag.
sol: Convert buoyancy energy to speed.
Kinetic energy per kg = ½w², set equal to CAPE.
w = √(2×2000) = 63.2 m/s. Trap: Real updrafts are well below this because of entrainment and drag.

new.q: [Meteorology | Setup: jets, fronts, shear | Tier 11] Surface wind is a 15 kt southerly (blowing northward) and the wind at 6 km is a 20 kt westerly (blowing eastward). What is the magnitude of the 0–6 km bulk shear (kt)?
new.w: Adding the speeds (35) forgets they are perpendicular.
sol: Shear is the VECTOR difference.
South wind and west wind are at right angles: use Pythagoras.
√(15² + 20²) = 25 kt. Trap: Adding the speeds (35) forgets they are perpendicular.

new.q: [Meteorology | Setup: jets, fronts, shear | Tier 11] The temperature drops 2 °C for every 100 km to your west, and the wind from the west is 50 km/h. How many °C per hour does cold advection cool a fixed point? (number only)

new.q: [Meteorology | Upper air, soundings, CAPE | Tier 12] A sounding has CAPE of 3500 J/kg but also a strong cap (large CIN). Why might no storms form by afternoon?
o: Parcels cannot get through the warm layer without lifting
High CAPE always guarantees that storms will form
CIN is simply another name for the CAPE value
The cap heats parcels until no energy is left
new.w: Equating high CAPE with guaranteed storms.
sol: Look for the stable layer.
CIN is the energy a parcel needs to overcome.
Storms need lifting (fronts, dryline, outflow) to get past the cap. Trap: Equating high CAPE with guaranteed storms.

new.q: [Meteorology | Setup: jets, fronts, shear | Tier 14] Winds turn clockwise with increasing height in the lowest 3 km. What is this called and why does it matter for supercells?
o: Veering, because it favours a rotating updraft
Backing, because it favours a rotating updraft
Veering, because it makes the updraft weaker
new.w: Swapping veering and backing is the most common vocabulary slip.
sol: Clockwise turning has a name.
Veering = clockwise; backing = counter-clockwise (in the Northern Hemisphere).
Veering with height supports a storm-relative inflow and rotation. Trap: Swapping veering and backing is the most common vocabulary slip.

new.q: [Meteorology | Tornadoes and radar | Tier 12] A radar scan shows strong inbound velocity directly beside strong outbound velocity. What does this couplet indicate?
o: A line of straight-line winds across the area
Large hail growing in the cloud aloft
A stationary front passing over the radar
new.w: Reading it as a uniform wind misses the opposite sign.
sol: Opposite directions side by side.
Doppler radar sees motion toward or away from the beam.
Adjacent opposite velocities mark rotation. Trap: Reading it as a uniform wind misses the opposite sign.

new.q: [Meteorology | Damaging winds | Tier 10] After a damaging wind event, trees are all laid in the same direction in a straight swath. Which was most likely?
o: A tornado with a narrow converging path
An earthquake shaking the trees down
A dust devil lifting debris upward
new.w: Assuming any severe wind damage is a tornado.
sol: Look at the pattern of damage.
Tornado damage converges or swirls; straight-line wind damage diverges outward in one direction.
Same-direction debris means divergent outflow. Trap: Assuming any severe wind damage is a tornado.

new.q: [Meteorology | Hurricanes | Tier 11] A hurricane moves north at 15 mph with maximum winds of 100 mph. Which quadrant usually has the strongest winds?
o: The right-front quadrant: motion adds to rotation
The left-rear quadrant, behind the storm
The middle of the eye at the centre
The left-front quadrant, ahead of the storm
new.w: Thinking the eye has the strongest wind – it is the calm center.
sol: Add vectors in the Northern Hemisphere, where the circulation is counter-clockwise.
On the right side, rotation and motion point the same way.
Right side: 100 + 15 = 115 mph; left: 100 − 15 = 85 mph. Trap: Thinking the eye has the strongest wind – it is the calm center.

new.q: [Meteorology | Hurricanes | Tier 8] Which condition most strongly weakens a hurricane?
new.w: Warm water and low pressure are growth factors, not weakeners.
sol: Shear tears the vertical structure.
A hurricane needs a tall, stacked circulation.
Shear tilts the storm and blows the heat release away from the center. Trap: Warm water and low pressure are growth factors, not weakeners.

sol: It is far less than people think.
Moving water as shallow as 6 inches can knock a person down; 12 inches floats many vehicles.
Remember: “Turn around, don’t drown.” Trap: Thinking a car is heavy enough to hold the ground.

new.q: [Meteorology | Winter storms | Tier 10] Rain falls through a deep warm layer and then a shallow layer below 0 °C at the surface. What reaches the ground?
new.w: Calling any ice sleet confuses which layer is sub-freezing.
sol: Check which layer is warm and which is cold.
Sleet needs a deep cold layer near the ground to refreeze drops first.
A shallow cold layer lets drops stay liquid until they hit a freezing surface. Trap: Calling any ice sleet confuses which layer is sub-freezing.

new.q: [Meteorology | Winter storms | Tier 10] For lake-effect snow, cold air flows across a warmer lake. About what temperature difference between the lake surface and 850 mb air is usually needed?
new.w: Using a tiny difference gives clouds but not heavy bands.
sol: It must be large enough for strong instability.
Rule of thumb for the Great Lakes.
A difference near 13 °C makes the low layer unstable enough for bands. Trap: Using a tiny difference gives clouds but not heavy bands.

new.q: [Meteorology | Drought and heat waves | Tier 9] A strong upper-level ridge sits over a region for days. Why do temperatures soar?
o: Sinking air warms by compression, skies clear
Rising air cools and leaves its heat behind
Cold air masses are pushed in from the north
The sun is closer to the ground at that time
new.w: Rising air cools, so it cannot explain a heat wave.
sol: Which way does air move in a ridge?
Sinking air is compressed and warmed adiabatically.
Subsidence also suppresses clouds and rain. Trap: Rising air cools, so it cannot explain a heat wave.

new.q: [Meteorology | Lightning | Tier 8] About how many strokes of lightning give the visible “flash”?
o: Several return strokes within a fraction of a second
Dozens of separate flashes per minute from one channel
None – it is all one continuous arc
new.w: Assuming one flash is one stroke.
sol: Flicker is real.
The first leader opens the channel; return strokes follow.
Multiple return strokes explain the flicker you see. Trap: Assuming one flash is one stroke.

new.q: [Meteorology | Observation tools | Tier 5] Each 10 dBZ increase in radar reflectivity means about how much more returned power?
new.w: Treating dB as a linear scale.
sol: dB scales are logarithmic.
10 dB is a factor of 10 in power.
So 50 dBZ returns 10× the power of 40 dBZ. Trap: Treating dB as a linear scale.

new.q: [Meteorology | Maps, station models, METAR | Tier 7] A METAR reads 27015G25KT. What does it say about the wind?
o: From 270° at 15 kt with gusts to 25 kt
From 270° at 25 kt with gusts to 15 kt
new.w: Reading direction as where the wind is going.
sol: Wind direction is where the wind comes FROM.
Direction (3 digits), speed (2), G for gust.
270° is westerly: from the west. Trap: Reading direction as where the wind is going.

new.q: [Meteorology | Maps, station models, METAR | Tier 6] On a station model, a wind barb has two full barbs and one half barb. What is the speed?
new.w: Counting a half barb as a full barb.
sol: Full barb 10 kt, half barb 5 kt.
Add them.
10 + 10 + 5 = 25 kt. Trap: Counting a half barb as a full barb.

new.q: [Meteorology | Hazards and safety | Tier 5] A tornado WARNING is issued for your town. What does it mean?
o: A tornado is happening or imminent: shelter now
Conditions are favourable: stay alert and be ready
A tornado was reported in the area last week
Winds will be strong but no tornado is expected
new.w: Mixing up watch and warning delays shelter.
sol: Watch vs warning.
A watch means favourable conditions; a warning means it is happening.
Warning = act now. Trap: Mixing up watch and warning delays shelter.

new.q: [Meteorology | Upper air, soundings, CAPE | Tier 10] A lifted index of −6 means what?
o: Unstable air that can support strong storms
Very stable air with no chance of storms
Air with no moisture in the whole column
A strong cold front passed through earlier
new.w: Reading the negative sign as “weak” instead of “unstable”.
sol: LI = environment temperature − lifted-parcel temperature at 500 mb.
Negative LI means the parcel is warmer than the environment.
The more negative, the more unstable. Trap: Reading the negative sign as “weak” instead of “unstable”.

new.q: [Meteorology | Severe thunderstorms | Tier 6] By NWS criteria, a thunderstorm is severe if it produces hail of at least what size?
new.w: Remembering the old ¾ inch criterion.
sol: It was raised from ¾ inch in 2010.
Quarter-sized hail.
Severe also means winds of 58 mph or higher or a tornado. Trap: Remembering the old ¾ inch criterion.

new.q: [Meteorology | Tornadoes and radar | Tier 8] A 140 mph tornado is rated what on the Enhanced Fujita scale?
new.w: Rating by damage vs wind speed ranges.
sol: EF3 is 136–165 mph.
Memorise the three-second-gust ranges.
EF0 65–85, EF1 86–110, EF2 111–135, EF3 136–165. Trap: Rating by damage vs wind speed ranges.

new.q: [Meteorology | Hurricanes | Tier 6] A hurricane has sustained winds of 120 mph. Which Saffir-Simpson category is it?
new.w: Assuming 120 is Category 4 because it is “big”.
sol: Cat 3 is 111–129 mph.
Learn the thresholds: 74, 96, 111, 130, 157.
120 falls between 111 and 129. Trap: Assuming 120 is Category 4 because it is “big”.

new.q: [Meteorology | Severe-weather clouds | Tier 9] A storm’s updraft is strong enough to push a flat anvil-like top above the tropopause. What is this called?
new.w: Confusing it with a wall cloud, which is on the base.
sol: The top is above the anvil.
It signals a very strong updraft.
Persistent overshooting tops mean an intense storm. Trap: Confusing it with a wall cloud, which is on the base.

new.q: [Meteorology | Severe-weather clouds | Tier 9] Which cloud lowering is usually found under the rain-free base of a supercell and may rotate?
new.w: A shelf cloud is on the leading edge of outflow and does not rotate.
sol: It sits beneath the updraft.
Wall clouds form from rain-cooled air near the updraft.
A rotating wall cloud often precedes a tornado. Trap: A shelf cloud is on the leading edge of outflow and does not rotate.

new.q: [Meteorology | Setup: jets, fronts, shear | Tier 10] Where does a dryline form in the Great Plains and why does it matter?
o: Between moist Gulf air and dry desert air
Between two cold air masses of equal moisture
Along the east coast where sea breezes meet
Between two jet streaks in the stratosphere
new.w: Treating the dryline as a temperature front.
sol: Look at the moisture contrast.
Dry air is denser than moist air at the same temperature.
Moist air is lifted over the dry air. Trap: Treating the dryline as a temperature front.

new.q: [Meteorology | Setup: jets, fronts, shear | Tier 11] Why are severe weather outbreaks often tied to a jet stream streak overhead?
o: Divergence aloft and strong wind shear
Direct heating of the surface air below
A fresh supply of moisture from the stratosphere
Removal of all cloud so the sun can heat
new.w: Thinking the jet directly heats the ground.
sol: Think upper-level support.
Jet streaks create divergence and shear.
Divergence aloft promotes rising air; shear organises storms. Trap: Thinking the jet directly heats the ground.

new.q: [Meteorology | Historic cases and data | Tier 10] A past outbreak lists large CAPE, strong shear, a cold front and a dryline. Which ingredient list is most complete for supercells?
o: Moisture, instability, lift and wind shear
Warm temperatures and clear blue skies
Cold air and a strong high pressure
Lightning and thunder showing on radar
new.w: Memorising only instability.
sol: There are four classic ingredients.
Moisture, instability, lift and shear.
Without any one of them, storms are weaker or do not form. Trap: Memorising only instability.
